extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of literary history and criticism (creative-writing students, literature undergraduates)
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and evaluative principles for judging medieval (and early modern) poetry and Gothic architecture, emphasizing symbolism, allegory, national spirit, formal features, and appropriate use of ornament and erudition. Useful for literary-critical assessments and creative-writing that draws on medieval modes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Simplicity of expression
rubrics_metrics.description: The first [peculiarity of the Bible] is simplicity of expression — the total want of all artifice. Although the sacred writings are principally or almost exclusively occupied with God and the internal being of man, their mode of treating these topics is everywhere lively and distinct; they contain little of what we are accustomed to call metaphysics; they are free from all those distinctions and antitheses, those dead ideas and empty abstractions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Value lively, distinct language that avoids artificial metaphysical hairsplitting, needless antitheses, and empty abstractions. The Scriptures provide an example: poetical parts possess sublime traits but sustain a simplicity that should be emulated rather than the 'ambitious and luxuriant taste' of overpolished classical models.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of symbolism and allegory
rubrics_metrics.description: A second peculiarity ... is that prevailing spirit of types and symbols so conspicuous ... the prevalence of a symbolizing spirit is still abundantly apparent. By means of this symbolical spirit, and the consequent propensity to allegory, the Bible has come to exert the same influence upon the poetry and all the imitative arts of the middle age ...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employ types, symbols, and allegory to deepen meaning and unify work; recognize the Bible as a model for symbolic density. But beware: where the deeper sense of symbolism is mistaken, the spirit can display itself in 'the corrupted form of idle and fantastical allegory.' Use allegory purposefully, not as mere ornament.

rubrics_metrics.name: Art must embody meaning / purposeful display of purpose
rubrics_metrics.description: Let a building be ever so beautiful, if it be destitute of meanings it cannot belong to the fine arts. The proper display of purpose, the immediate expression of feeling, is indeed denied to this oldest and most sublime of all the arts; it must excite the feelings through the medium of thought.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Whether architecture or literature, works must express thought and purpose — they should not be mere assemblages of form. Prioritize intelligible intentions and symbolic content that stimulate feeling via intellectual depth rather than empty decoration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Architectural features expressing spiritual elevation
rubrics_metrics.description: That style of Christian architecture ... characterized by its lofty vaults and arches; its pillars, which have the appearance of being formed out of bundles of reeds; its profusion of ornament; its flowers and leaves ... The first and greatest of its objects is to express the elevation of holy thoughts, the loftiness of meditation set free from earth, and proceeding unfettered to the heavens.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In Gothic-inspired design (and analogous poetic strategies), assess presence of verticality, soaring vaults, clustered columns, profuse organic ornament, and recurring motifs (the rose) as formal means to evoke spiritual elevation and contemplative loftiness. These formal choices should coherently serve expressive ends.

rubrics_metrics.name: Integration of symbolic elements in structure
rubrics_metrics.description: Every part of the structure is as symbolical as the whole ... The altar is directed towards the rising of the sun, and the three great entrances are meant to express the conflux of worshippers from all the regions of the earth. Three towers express the Christian mystery of the triune Godhead. The choir rises like a temple within a temple ... The rose is the essential part of all the ornament of this architecture.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether individual elements (orientation, entrances, towers, plan-shapes, recurring decorative motifs) coherently contribute to an overall symbolic program. Coherence and purpose in small details reinforce the work's communicative power; arbitrary or decorative insertions weaken it.

rubrics_metrics.name: National spirit and embodiment of nationality
rubrics_metrics.description: The literature of Spain possesses a high advantage ... A single work, such as the Cid, is of more real value to a nation than a whole library of books ... which are destitute of the spirit of nationality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prize works that concretely embody and preserve a nation's feelings and character; such works have enduring cultural value and influence. Creative-writing aiming for national resonance should draw from authentic traditions and popular memory rather than contrived exoticism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance of imagination and historical grounding in heroic poetry
rubrics_metrics.description: The chivalrous poetry of a former age erred in entirely departing from history, and becoming a mere display of imagination; the poets now ran into the opposite extreme, and composed regular chronicles in rhyme. Thus the two elements of true heroic poetry were given not in conjunction, but in detail.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Strong heroic poetry should blend imaginative, mythic elements with a credible historical or real-world grounding. Avoid pure fantasy unmoored from history, and equally avoid dry chronicle devoid of imaginative force.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accessibility combined with poetic richness in popular ballads
rubrics_metrics.description: They are not only popular ballads, intelligible and clear to the vulgar, they are also true national and heroic poems, which may be read with the highest admiration by the most refined critics. It is always to be regretted when that poetry ... assumes a form which adapts it only for the vulgar. Such poetry ... becomes every day more unintelligible even to those for whose use it is formed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aim for clarity and intelligibility that serves a broad audience while retaining depth and artistic merit that satisfies critical readers. Avoid dumbed-down forms tailored only to immediate popular taste that will age into unintelligibility or triviality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Modes of allegorical composition (embedded vs. world-embracing)
rubrics_metrics.description: The difference consists in this, that in these allegorical romances the hidden sense is wrapped up in a representation of human life and transactions, while in Dante, on the contrary, the representations of human life are only inserted here and there as adventitious pieces of furniture in the artfully divided saloons and galleries of this world-embracing allegory.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize two productive uses of allegory: (a) narratives with a concealed moral sense woven into ordinary action, and (b) totally allegorical, systemized world-views (Dante). Choose the mode that suits subject and aim; ensure that allegory enhances rather than overwhelms intelligibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Judge works by their own time and accompanying arts
rubrics_metrics.description: I am far from admiring the custom of those who are perpetually tracing resemblances between the poets of different countries and ages. If we must compare the poems of that age to something, let it be, not to the poems of other times, but to the other works of art which were produced in their own time, and in their own country.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid anachronistic or cross-era comparisons that ignore historical context. Evaluate a work relative to the aesthetic aims, materials, and other arts of its own period and culture.

rubrics_metrics.name: Value of the unfinished/undefined in enhancing grandeur
rubrics_metrics.description: It may be, that the grandeur of the original conception comes upon us with a stronger impulse from this unfinished work than it might have done had they been adorned with the last exquisite touches of elegance. The terrible graces are ever conversant with the undefined.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider that incomplete or 'rough' features can intensify imaginative impact and grandeur; over-finishing may reduce power. Resist over-polishing when a degree of openness or mystery serves the work's emotional or symbolic aims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dangers of excessive ornament and over-loaded artifice
rubrics_metrics.description: To the highest polish of art there succeeds, not unfrequently, an ambitious and luxuriant taste which delights in superfluous ornament and over-loaded artifice. There exist many causes ... which may poison and corrode the bloom of beauty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat restraint as a virtue: avoid superfluous ornamentation and pedantic complexity that obscure native grace. Let ornament serve meaning; do not allow technique or erudition to overwhelm aesthetic truth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Religion as groundwork, not ordinary poetic subject
rubrics_metrics.description: Christianity ... is, according to my opinion, no proper subject of poetry; I except lyrical compositions, which are to be considered as direct emanations of feeling. Christianity itself cannot be either philosophy or poetry. It is rather what ought to be the groundwork of all philosophy ... the influence of our sublime faith should indeed be every where around us, but here its ministrations should be felt, not seen, and we should beware of debasing, by familiarity, that which is most worthy of our reverence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use religious belief as an underpinning influence shaping tone, values, and symbolism, rather than as a literal topic for poetic treatment (except for intimate lyrical expression). Avoid treating sacred doctrine as commonplace subject-matter that risks debasement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Linguistic maturity and historical circumstances affect literary quality
rubrics_metrics.description: The French literature of the fourteenth century is indeed extremely poor; but from the romances and what other productions of that period we have in our hands, it appears that the language had at that time a character very inferior in every respect to the contemporary dialects of Spain and Italy. ... the long wars ... prevented, in a great measure, the natural progress both of language and poetry.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating literature, account for the development and uniformity of language and historical disruptions (wars, political fragmentation) that shape literary production. Weaknesses in style or form may reflect linguistic immaturity or social conditions rather than individual failure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriate synthesis of classical learning and native feeling
rubrics_metrics.description: Boccaccio ... endeavoured to embody the hairsplitting fancifulness of the Provencial love-queries and love-cases of conscience, and the amusing fictions of the Norman story-tellers, in a style of composition far too serious, too elaborate, and too ornate for his purpose. ... he indulges in the same fruitless endeavours to reconcile [the antique] with those poetical feelings which are peculiar to the modern world.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aim to harmonize classical erudition with indigenous forms of feeling and subject-matter. Avoid forced antique affectation or learned ornament that misfits the spirit of the material; let learning serve native imaginative needs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Erudition should not overshadow poetic originality
rubrics_metrics.description: Wolkram ... bears no small resemblance to that illustrious poet, both in his propensity to allegories, and in his love of displaying, with some little pedantry, what was in those times a greater rarity than genius itself — his extensive erudition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Value genuine creative power over mere learned display. Excessive pedantry or ostentatious learning can detract from the poet's imaginative force; use erudition to enrich rather than to parade.
